content: Paneth cells are specialized epithelial cells located in the small intestine that play a critical role in host defense against microbial pathogens. These cells are functionally analogous to neutrophils, as they actively respond to bacterial exposure or bacterial antigens by secreting a variety of antimicrobial molecules into the lumen of the intestinal crypts. This secretion contributes significantly to the maintenance of the gastrointestinal barrier, ensuring the integrity of the intestinal epithelium. Paneth cells are named after Joseph Paneth, an Austrian physician who lived from 1857 to 1890. The crypts of the small intestine house stem cells that are essential for the continuous replenishment of epithelial cells, which are regularly lost from the villi due to natural turnover. The protection of these stem cells is vital for the long-term maintenance of the intestinal epithelium. The strategic positioning of Paneth cells adjacent to these stem cells suggests that Paneth cells play a pivotal role in safeguarding the renewal and regeneration of epithelial cells. The primary antimicrobial molecules secreted by Paneth cells are alpha-defensins, also referred to as cryptdins. These peptides possess both hydrophobic and positively charged domains, which enable them to interact with phospholipids in cell membranes. This structural property allows defensins to insert themselves into membranes, where they aggregate to form pores. These pores disrupt membrane integrity, ultimately leading to cell lysis. Due to the higher concentration of negatively charged phospholipids in bacterial membranes compared to vertebrate cell membranes, defensins preferentially bind to and disrupt bacterial cells while sparing the host cells they are designed to protect. Paneth cells are stimulated to secrete defensins in response to exposure to bacteria, including both Gram-positive and Gram-negative types, as well as bacterial products such as lipopolysaccharide, muramyl dipeptide, and lipid A. In addition to defensins, Paneth cells secrete other antimicrobial molecules, including lysozyme and phospholipase A2. Both of these enzymes exhibit potent antimicrobial activity. This diverse array of secretory molecules equips Paneth cells with a robust arsenal to combat a wide range of pathogens, including bacteria, fungi, and even certain enveloped viruses.
